She just parked in the sky. And nobody in that crowd will ever complain about traffic the same way again.

I need you to sit with that for one second before you scroll.

Because what you're looking at is not a car. It's not a drone. It's not a concept render some studio built to farm engagement (well — actually it kind of is, but stay with me, that's not the point). It's the first physical proof that the single most mocked promise in the history of technology — "where's my flying car" — is no longer a punchline. It's a delivery date.

For eighty years, "flying car" has been the go-to insult for broken promises. Every futurist, every 1960s World's Fair pamphlet, every Popular Mechanics cover from 1950 swore we'd all be commuting through the clouds by the year 2000. We got the internet instead. We got smartphones instead. We got a species that can video-call anyone on Earth for free but still sits in a metal box for ninety minutes a day, staring at brake lights, burning the one resource none of us can print more of: time.

And somewhere along the way "flying car" stopped meaning innovation and started meaning delusion. It became shorthand for every grifter with a PowerPoint. Ask any cynic what technology never arrived and they'll say it before you finish the question. It's the punchline that killed a thousand pitch decks.

Except punchlines don't get certified by aviation regulators. Punchlines don't raise nine-figure funding rounds. Punchlines don't have five-figure order books before a single unit has shipped.

This one does.

Let me give you the numbers, because the numbers are the part nobody's talking about while everyone's busy arguing about whether the render looks "fake."

There is a Chinese automaker's flying-car division that has already logged over 5,000 pre-orders for a modular eVTOL — a vehicle that drives like a normal car and detaches into a two-seat aircraft when you need it to. Mass production isn't a "someday." It's scheduled. Deliveries begin in the second half of this year. Price target: under two million yuan, translating to roughly $280,000 at today's exchange rate — which sounds insane until you remember that's the price of a nice house in most cities, and this thing gets you out of the city entirely, vertically, without needing a runway.

Across the ocean, an American company backed by $900 million from one of the largest automakers on the planet is expanding a factory to build two dozen aircraft a year — with a second facility gearing up to eventually push that number to 500 annually. They're partnered with a major airline for airport-to-downtown routes. The pitch is simple and devastating: land at the airport, skip the taxi line, skip the highway, skip the hour of gridlock between the runway and your hotel, and be standing in Midtown before your checked bag even hits the carousel.

A rival is doing the same thing in Abu Dhabi and Dubai — cities that have money, space, and zero interest in waiting for anyone else to go first.

Analysts are projecting this category to be worth over a trillion dollars a year by 2040. Not a niche. Not a toy for tech bros. A trillion-dollar transportation layer stacked directly on top of the one we've been stuck using since 1908.

Read that last sentence again. 1908. That's the year Ford put the Model T into mass production. That is the actual, factual last time humanity fundamentally reinvented how the average person gets from point A to point B. Everything since then — better engines, GPS, ride-share apps, electric drivetrains — has been optimization. Same layer. Same roads. Same rules. Same traffic.

We didn't get a new layer. We got a faster horse with better upholstery.

Until now.

And here's the part that should actually unsettle you, not excite you: the bottleneck was never the technology. It wasn't the batteries. It wasn't the motors. It wasn't the materials. Vertical takeoff, electric propulsion, autonomous flight stabilization — all of that has existed, in workable form, for the better part of a decade. Military drones have been doing autonomous vertical flight since before the iPhone had a front camera.

The bottleneck was permission. Regulation. Certification. Airspace law written for Boeing 747s trying to figure out what to do with a two-seat vehicle that takes off from a sidewalk. The bottleneck was humans, not machines. And bureaucracy, it turns out, moves slower than propellers.

That bottleneck is now breaking. Not "might break." Breaking. Right now. This year. Certification bodies in multiple countries are actively processing applications for passenger eVTOL operations. Test flights are happening in Dubai, in Shenzhen, in California. The paperwork that stood between "cool prototype" and "thing you can legally own" is being signed as you read this.

So let's talk about what actually happens when the paperwork clears. Because I don't think most people have thought this through, and I think that's exactly why this video stopped your scroll.

Phase one is what you'd expect. It's a luxury flex. A six-figure toy for the same demographic that currently buys a Cullinan or a Patek Philippe just to say they can. Nobody needs a $280,000 watch either. Status has never required necessity. The first wave of owners aren't buying transportation — they're buying the single most undeniable proof of "I made it" available on the market, because unlike a car, unlike a watch, unlike a private jet you still have to schedule and taxi and wait for clearance on — this thing lifts off a sidewalk in front of everyone who told you it couldn't be done.

That's not a flex. That's a public execution of every person who ever doubted you, staged in under four seconds, with witnesses.

Phase two is where it gets uncomfortable. Because luxury goods don't stay luxury. They stay expensive for the people who need the status, and they get cheap for everyone else, on a curve that's gotten steeper every single decade since the industrial revolution. The first commercial airline ticket in 1914 cost the equivalent of a used car today, for a twenty-three-minute hop across Tampa Bay. The first mobile phone cost $4,000 in 1983 money and got you thirty minutes of talk time before it died. The first LCD television cost more than most cars.

Look at your pocket right now. Look at what's sitting in it. That's what happens to "impossible luxury" on a long enough timeline. It becomes normal. It becomes invisible. It becomes the thing your kids assume has always existed, the same way you assume WiFi has always existed, the same way your grandparents assumed cars had always existed.

Batteries are already crossing the energy-density thresholds this category needs. Manufacturing capacity in China alone is being built for over 10,000 units a year at a single facility. That is not boutique production. That is the exact same industrial playbook that took electric cars from "rich person's science project" to "one in five new cars sold worldwide" in under fifteen years. The people building these vehicles are the same supply chains, the same battery giants, the same manufacturing muscle that just did this once already, in real time, in front of everyone who said it couldn't scale.

They're not guessing. They've done this before.

So here's the timeline nobody wants to say out loud because it sounds insane until you actually map it against precedent: ten years from luxury flex to six-figure early adopter. Fifteen to twenty from six-figure early adopter to the price of a decent SUV. Twenty-five to thirty and your kid's driving instructor is teaching two separate tests, because the sky above every mid-sized city has a marked traffic lane and a speed limit, exactly the way the ground does now.

I know how that sentence reads. I know it sounds like the same breathless "flying cars by the year 2000" hype that made this whole category a joke in the first place. But go back and read the difference. The 1960s promise had no working prototype, no certified aircraft, no order book, no factory, no funding round, no regulatory pathway being actively processed by a real government agency in real time. This one has all five. That's not vibes. That's not a render. That's not marketing. Those are checkboxes, and they're getting checked on a public timeline you can go verify yourself in about four minutes of searching.

Now play forward the part that actually matters — not the vehicle, the society underneath it.

What happens to a city's real estate when the commute stops being a two-dimensional problem? Right now, "close to downtown" is the single biggest price multiplier on every property listing on Earth, because proximity is currency when your only travel axis is roads clogged with everyone else's cars. The moment vertical travel becomes normal, "close" stops meaning miles. It starts meaning minutes, in a straight line, over everything in between. A house forty miles out with a clear flight path becomes more valuable, overnight, than a house four miles out buried behind three points of gridlock. That is a multi-trillion-dollar repricing of literally every parcel of land on the planet, and almost nobody is pricing it in yet.

What happens to emergency response when an ambulance doesn't need a road at all? What happens to disaster relief when the flood or the earthquake takes out every bridge and every highway and the only vehicles still able to move are the ones that were never using the ground to begin with? What happens to rural medicine, rural logistics, rural anything, when distance from a highway stops being a life-or-death variable?

What happens to a hundred years of infrastructure spending — the roads, the bridges, the interchanges, the entire trillion-dollar skeleton every government on Earth maintains — when the fastest-growing segment of transportation needs almost none of it?

What happens to insurance? To licensing? To the entire concept of a "commute," a word that currently means something closer to captivity for the average worker in almost every major city on the planet? What happens to a generation raised watching their parents lose two unpaid hours a day to a steering wheel, the second they realize that was never actually mandatory — it was just the only option that existed yet?

I'm not asking these questions because I have all the answers. Nobody does. I'm asking them because the fact that we're even asking them, seriously, with funding rounds and factories and pre-order books attached, is the actual story here. Not the paint color. Not the door mechanism. Not whether the render looks convincing enough for your skeptical uncle in the replies.

The story is that the ceiling just moved. Literally. For the first time in over a century, "up" is a real answer to "how do I get there," not a science-fiction one.

And I get the instinct to dunk on it. I get the "yeah right, in MY city, where they can't even fix a pothole" energy. I get the "this'll never happen because of regulation / insurance / noise / rich people ruining the sky too" pushback, and honestly? Some of that pushback is completely fair. Noise pollution over dense cities is a real, unsolved problem. Airspace congestion at scale is a real, unsolved problem. The idea of untrained pilots navigating three-dimensional traffic above a school is a legitimately terrifying regulatory nightmare that deserves to be terrifying, because getting it wrong doesn't total a car, it ends lives, and any serious rollout has to earn public trust before it earns market share. Every single one of these objections is a real obstacle, and every single one of them is currently being worked by aviation regulators, insurance actuaries, and airspace engineers whose entire job is exactly this. That's not hope. That's an industry with a literal budget line item for solving it.

But "hard" is not the same as "impossible," and the entire history of transportation is a graveyard of experts who confused the two. Cars were "too dangerous, too loud, too expensive, roads will never be built for them." Planes were "physically impossible, and even if they weren't, no sane person would ever fly commercially." The internet was "a fad for hobbyists, real business will always run on paper and phone calls." Every single one of those quotes is real. Every single one of those experts was catastrophically, historically wrong, and every single one of them was wrong for the same reason: they were extrapolating the present instead of the curve.

You're standing at the same fork right now. You can look at that clip and think "cute concept, never happening here," and I promise you, ten years from now, you will not remember writing that comment, but the timeline will remember it happened anyway, the same way nobody remembers doubting the smartphone but everybody has one.

Or you can actually feel what that four-second clip is telling you, underneath the spectacle. Somebody just stepped out of gridlock. Permanently. Somebody just deleted the single most universally hated part of the human day — the part every commuter on Earth would trade almost anything to skip — and did it in front of a crowd who are all still standing there, on the ground, watching, phones up, exactly where they were five minutes ago, exactly where they'll be tomorrow, and the day after, and every weekday for the rest of their working lives, unless something changes.

That's the part that should actually get under your skin. Not the paint. Not the doors. Not the price tag. The fact that everyone in that crowd is currently living inside the exact same broken system you are, and one person just showed them, in real time, that the walls of that system are not load-bearing. They're just old. They're just the way it's always been, right up until the second somebody with enough capital, enough engineering, and enough conviction decides it doesn't have to be.

Every transportation revolution in human history has looked exactly like this in year one. A small, expensive, slightly absurd-looking prototype that the majority of onlookers laugh at, while a tiny minority quietly starts writing checks and pre-orders and doing the math on a fifteen-year curve nobody else is bothering to run. The people who laughed at the Model T in 1908 were technically right that most people couldn't afford one yet. They were catastrophically wrong about what "yet" meant.

So here's my actual question for you, and I mean this one seriously, not rhetorically: when the price on this category crosses into "aggressive but achievable" territory — and every curve in every comparable category says it will, and probably faster than you're currently assuming — are you going to be the person who saw it coming from a decade out, who tracked the funding rounds and the certification milestones and the pre-order numbers and positioned early, in whatever way that means for you? Or are you going to be the person standing on the sidewalk again, phone up, filming somebody else doing what you spent ten years insisting was fake?

Because I've watched this exact movie play out with electric cars, with smartphones, with the internet itself, and it is always, always the same two characters in the same two roles. The ones who called it early, and the ones who called it fake right up until they were quietly downloading the app, buying the stock, or standing in line for the thing they swore they'd never want.

The sky isn't full yet. That's the whole point. That's the entire opportunity compressed into one sentence. Every road on Earth is full. Every highway on Earth is full. Every single square foot of ground-level transportation infrastructure on this planet has been full, functionally, for decades, which is why your commute hasn't meaningfully improved since before you were born no matter how much money any government throws at it.

The sky is still empty. Completely, almost insultingly empty, for a species that figured out powered flight over a century ago and then, somehow, mostly kept it reserved for people wearing a captain's uniform and flying between airports two hundred miles apart. That's the actual gap. Not a technology gap. Not even really a regulatory gap anymore, not for much longer. A usage gap. The single most under-utilized piece of infrastructure available to the human race is the three hundred feet of open air directly above every traffic jam on Earth, and for the first time in history, the machines that can legally, safely, and affordably use it are not a decade away in some lab. They have order books. They have factories. They have delivery windows written down on a calendar with a real year attached to them.

You just watched someone use it like it was nothing. Like it was a normal Tuesday. That's not a stunt. That's a preview, running about a decade ahead of schedule, of what "normal Tuesday" is going to look like for everyone else, whether the sidewalk crowd is ready to believe it yet or not.

Save this post. Not because you need to reread it — because in a few years, when this stops looking like science fiction and starts looking like the parking lot outside your office, I want you to remember exactly how impossible it felt the first time you scrolled past it. That feeling is the whole story. Every transformative technology in human history has made people feel exactly that, right before it became the most ordinary thing in the world.

The commute you're sitting in right now was never the ceiling. It was just the only floor anyone had built yet.

They just started building the next one. Straight up.

Now let me address the replies before you even write them, because I've had this exact argument a hundred times and it always breaks down the same predictable way.

"This is fake, it's CGI." Sure, the clip you're watching might be a rendered concept, a marketing reel, a controlled demo — I'm not going to pretend to know the provenance of every viral video that crosses a timeline, and neither should you. But that's exactly why I didn't build this post around the clip. I built it around the paper trail underneath it: the order books, the funding rounds, the factories under construction, the certification filings sitting in front of real regulators right now. You can doubt a video. It is significantly harder to doubt a nine-figure Series B, a signed airline partnership, and a factory with a stated annual capacity in the five figures. Fake videos don't raise real capital. Real capital is exactly what's raising here.

"Nobody's going to let untrained people fly two feet over a crowded sidewalk." Correct. Nobody serious is proposing that either. Every credible player in this space is targeting designated corridors, automated flight paths, geofenced takeoff and landing zones, and — in the earliest phases — licensed or semi-licensed operation, not "buy it Tuesday, freestyle it Wednesday." The rollout looks a lot more like how drones actually got regulated than like a Hollywood chase scene. Boring, incremental, corridor by corridor, city by city. Boring is what "actually happening" looks like. Spectacular is what movies look like. This is the boring version, and that's exactly why it's real.

"The noise will be unbearable." This is the single most legitimate objection in the entire conversation, and I want to give it the respect it deserves instead of hand-waving it away. Early rotor-based eVTOLs are not silent. But the acoustic profile of a small electric multi-rotor aircraft is not remotely comparable to a helicopter, and several manufacturers in this space have specifically engineered blade count, rotor speed, and distributed propulsion around cutting the perceived noise footprint dramatically below rotorcraft baselines — some publicly targeting noise levels that blend into ordinary urban background sound rather than cutting through it. Is that solved everywhere, for every design, at scale? No. Is it a dealbreaker that kills the category? Also no. It's an engineering constraint being actively optimized, the same way EV range anxiety was an engineering constraint being actively optimized ten years ago, right up until it quietly stopped being a conversation at all.

"This is only for the ultra-rich, it'll never trickle down." I already walked through the pricing curve on electric cars, smartphones, flat-screen TVs, and commercial air travel above, and I'll say it again because it's the single most reliable pattern in the entire history of consumer technology: nothing expensive stays expensive once manufacturing scales. Ever. Not once, not in any category, not in the last hundred years. The only variable that ever changes is the timeline, and the timeline compresses every single decade because the tools for scaling manufacturing get better every single decade too. The iPhone took the entire smartphone category from luxury to ubiquity in about a decade. Solar panels dropped in cost by over ninety percent in fifteen years. Batteries are on the same curve right now, today, and the entire flying-car category is downstream of battery economics. Betting against that curve has been the single worst bet in technology for a hundred years running.

"City infrastructure isn't ready." Also true, also not the point. Nothing is ever "ready" the moment a technology arrives — infrastructure follows adoption, it doesn't precede it. There were no gas stations when the first Model T rolled off the line either. There was no cellular network worth using when the first iPhone shipped. The chicken-and-egg problem is real, and it's also never once stopped a transformative technology from getting built anyway, because the first movers don't wait for perfect infrastructure — they build the minimum viable version of it themselves, on purpose, specifically to force everyone else to catch up. Vertiports are already being planned and built in multiple major cities right now, for exactly this reason, years before mass adoption, because the companies involved have read this same history and know exactly how the story goes.

Here's the pattern I want you to actually take away from this, stripped of all the specifics: every single objection people are raising about flying cars right now is a real, legitimate, currently-unsolved engineering or regulatory problem. And every single one of those objections has an exact, direct historical parallel that was raised, in the same tone, with the same confidence, about every transportation and communication technology that has ever gone on to become invisible and ordinary. Not most. Every one. Cars, planes, phones, the internet, GPS, ride-sharing, electric vehicles. The graveyard of "this will never work, here's why" takes is the single most crowded graveyard in the history of technological commentary, and it keeps getting new residents every single year, right on schedule, from people who are usually smart, usually well-informed, and usually wrong for exactly the same reason: they're measuring a launching rocket by how it looks on the pad.

Let me leave you with the actual comparison that matters, because I think it's the one that finally makes this click for people who've read this far and are still not sure whether to believe any of it.

In 1903, two bicycle mechanics from Ohio got a machine into the air for twelve seconds, a hundred and twenty feet, at a windswept beach nobody had heard of. Most of the serious scientific establishment at the time considered heavier-than-air flight a mathematical impossibility — there were peer-reviewed papers, from credentialed physicists, explaining exactly why it couldn't be done, published within years of it being done. Sixty-six years later, three men rode a controlled explosion to the surface of the Moon and walked around on it while a television audience of half a billion people watched live from their living rooms.

Sixty-six years. One human lifetime. From "this is mathematically impossible" to "we're casually doing this for a live broadcast."

We are currently standing at the exact equivalent of 1903 for personal vertical flight. Not the metaphorical equivalent — the literal one. A working prototype. A skeptical public. A wall of confident experts explaining exactly why it won't scale. And a small group of engineers who are demonstrably, provably not listening to any of them, because they're too busy building the next iteration.

I'm not telling you to believe the hype uncritically. I'm telling you to notice the shape of the argument you're having, because you've had it before, on the other side, about something you now consider completely unremarkable. The commute is not a law of physics. It's an infrastructure choice, made over a century ago, that nobody has seriously challenged at scale until right now, in this exact window, with real capital and real hardware behind it for the first time in eighty years of broken promises.

You don’t have to believe me but please do fact check me.

IFF's statement on the AI Impact Summit 2026.

The Internet Freedom Foundation (IFF) welcomes the India AI Impact Summit 2026 (February 16-20) as an important platform for global dialogue on, "Artificial Intelligence". We believe the Summit's agenda and framing fundamentally misalign with the lived reality of AI deployment in India, an environment marked by rising digital authoritarianism and the systematic erosion of constitutional protections that are causing demonstrable harm to vulnerable populations. Its official framing centers on “People, Planet and Progress”, with Prime Minister Narendra Modi inaugurating and world leaders like France’s President Emmanuel Macron and top tech CEOs (Google’s Sundar Pichai, OpenAI’s Sam Altman, etc.) expected to attend. The Summit's optimistic narrative about AI for development obscures the reality of how its deployment is impacting people in their everyday lives.

The current environment is one of a sharp contraction in civic space, where recent governance proposals on technology have facilitated the expansion of state power that run contrary to the state commitments on fundamental rights and social justice. Today, there exists few organisations in India that work on digital rights and those which are surviving are severely under resourced, suffer from burdensome compliances, growing legal risks and deliberate exclusion from policy making processes. The decline of civil society work is matching the growth of private and public sector capacity to lobby the policy making processes. So, even before a question is prompted, how should Indian civil society engage with the India AI Impact Summit, a predicate and grounded inquiry is, how many independent, Indian civil society groups exist in India that have capacity and can be critical of state policies and practices around AI?

In the recent past, far from fostering accountability, India’s digitisation drive is often used to sidestep constitutional safeguards of transparency, harming communities and individuals. For instance, recent legal changes have weakened the Right to Information (RTI) framework, curtailing citizens’ ability to question power. The Digital Personal Data Protection (DPDP) Act, 2023 introduced an amendment (Section 8(1)(j) to the RTI Act) that blocks access to any information labeled “personal information”, allowing officials to deny critical information. Likewise, digitisation of welfare governance has been weaponized to bypass accountability, with digitisation often becoming a gatekeeper and working to the detriment of the poor. A stark development came in December, 2025 when Parliament hastily passed the Viksit Bharat - Guarantee for Rozgar and Ajeevika Mission (Gramin) Act, 2025 (VB-GRAM G), repealing the landmark MGNREGA jobs guarantee program. VB-GRAM G converted a demand driven legal right to work into a discretionary, bureaucratically controlled scheme, undermining decades of workers’ rights. There are references to "AI" within the text of the objects and reasons that are a part of this law.

Beyond this, India's policies on AI also demonstrate a wider embrace of de-regulation narratives to ensure, "innovation". For instance, the Union Budget 2026 unveiled a 20-year tax holiday (until 2047) for foreign firms using Indian data centers, aiming to lure global AI infrastructure. Yet, this policy was formulated with scant regard for its impact on local communities and natural resources. Other recent measures also deserve comment:

Sanchar Saathi : In late 2025, the government ordered smartphone manufacturers to pre-install a government cybersecurity application called Sanchar Saathi on all devices. The app was ostensibly meant to secure citizens’ phones, but the mandatory installation sparked outrage over privacy and surveillance concerns, drawing parallels to spyware abuse.
The ‘Sahyog’ Censorship Portal: In 2024, the Union Home Ministry quietly launched the Sahyog Portal to expedite content-blocking orders on social media and websites. Under this system, law enforcement agencies can flag “unlawful” online content and directly trigger its takedown by internet platforms, all through a centralized interface.
Expansion of NATGRID: Perhaps the most far-reaching is the quiet expansion of NATGRID, India’s National Intelligence Grid. Long conceived as an integrated database for counter-terror investigations, NATGRID has recently morphed into a broad surveillance net. Following a high-level police conference in late November 2025, states were directed to “scale up” NATGRID usage beyond central agencies, even giving police officers at the Superintendent rank access to its vast datasets.
These developments match the increased use of AI technologies in domains of policing and welfare without a clear legal basis and real safeguards.

IFF acknowledges that the India AI Impact Summit 2026 offers a platform for dialogue and a chance for civil society voices to gain visibility on an international stage. We recognize the value in having digital rights perspectives included in global AI governance conversations, indeed, the Summit’s presence in India is an opportunity to spotlight our constitutional concerns before a world audience. We support our peer organizations and allies who choose to engage with the Summit, and we will remain in constructive collaboration with them. However, IFF has decided not to allocate significant organizational resources to direct participation in the Summit’s events. This is not a boycott of the forum, but a practical choice of focus. As a small team of only 7 full-time staff based in New Delhi, we must prioritize the most pressing advocacy initiatives that align closely with our mission and charter.

This includes ongoing efforts such as legal challenges to unconstitutional regulations, campaigning and community engagement for strengthening free expression, privacy and transparency frameworks. These are battles immediately affecting citizens’ rights and requiring our sustained attention. IFF will engage with the Summit in a mindful, critical manner. We will track the proceedings and outcomes closely, offering our analyses and critiques rooted in constitutional values. If and where we do participate (for example, in side events or discussions), we will do so with a critical gaze, centering the lived experiences of Indians and the paramountcy of our fundamental rights. Our support is firmly with the broader civil society coalition pushing for AI governance that is accountable and just.

A disturbing question has emerged around the Special Intensive Revision (SIR) and Form 6—the form used by citizens to register as new voters.

The video argues that changes were made to Form 6 without the approval of the other Election Commissioners and warns that this could create difficulties for future first-time voters. 

That is no longer merely a social-media claim.

The Indian Express has reported that Election Commissioners Sukhbir Singh Sandhu and Vivek Joshi formally objected to the changes. According to the investigation, Form 6 was modified to ask new applicants whether their own, or their parent/grandparent's, name appeared in an earlier SIR electoral roll. The two Commissioners questioned the legal basis for changing the statutory form without amending the relevant rules. 

The reported objections go beyond Form 6. The two Commissioners also raised concerns about the centralisation of electoral-roll databases, access by state-level officials, voter-deletion appeals in West Bengal and software-related problems in Goa. 

At the same time, the Election Commission has rejected the suggestion that its final SIR decisions were divided, saying that differences and written observations are part of institutional deliberation and that decisions were unanimous. 

So the central democratic question is simple:

If the system is completely transparent and lawful, why should citizens be denied clear answers about who authorised the changes, under what legal authority, and how dissenting objections were dealt with?

Electoral reform should never be about protecting one party or attacking another.

The voter comes first.
The electoral roll must be transparent.
And the Election Commission must be accountable to the Constitution—not to political power.

10 QUESTIONS THE ECI MUST ANSWER ON SIR, FORM 6 & THE VOTER DATABASE

https://t.co/A395nzA0Kw

The Election Commission of India has said that all its decisions, including those relating to the Special Intensive Revision (SIR), were unanimous, and that differences of opinion among Commissioners are a normal part of institutional deliberation. 

But the questions raised by The Indian Express investigation—and examined in this video by Sanket Upadhyay—deserve specific answers, not merely general assurances.

According to the investigation, Election Commissioners Sukhbir Singh Sandhu and Vivek Joshi recorded at least 14 formal objections over 10 months concerning electoral-roll decisions. The reported concerns included new-voter registration, voter deletions, access to the electoral database, appeals in West Bengal and the functioning of the Commission's IT systems. 

THE QUESTIONS THAT MATTER

1. FORM 6:
Why was a new SIR-related question added to Form 6 for first-time voters when the two Commissioners had reportedly objected that the change required a rule amendment? 

2. WHO AUTHORISED IT?
If the change was legally authorised, what was the precise legal authority and approval process?

3. 14 OBJECTIONS:
Were the reported objections made before or after the relevant decisions were formally taken—and how were they resolved?

4. ECI COMMUNICATIONS:
Why did the two Commissioners reportedly question communications issued in the name of the ECI without their approval?

5. ECINET & ERO POWERS:
If Electoral Registration Officers retain their statutory powers, why were concerns raised that the centralised software restricted their ability to act?

6. GOA'S 97 VOTERS:
The Indian Express reported that Goa EROs found 97 voters eligible, but the software did not allow their decisions to be recorded before the final roll. What exactly happened? 

7. WEST BENGAL'S 16.10 LAKH APPEALS:
Who authorised the appeals filed against voters whom judicial officers had included, and who actually filed them?

8. CABINET SECRETARY:
Why did the two Election Commissioners reportedly write separately to the Cabinet Secretary over changes affecting IT oversight? 

9. FOUR-MONTH GAP:
How could decisions be described as unanimous if the full three-member Commission reportedly did not meet for four months? The ECI's explanation needs to address the chronology directly.

10. INDEPENDENT AUDIT:
If concerns were raised about who can alter the electoral database, why was the proposed audit not carried out—or, if it was, where are its findings?

These questions do not by themselves establish electoral manipulation or illegality. The ECI disputes the interpretation of the reported internal differences and says its decisions were unanimous. 

But democracy depends on something more fundamental than competing narratives:

A voter should not have to choose between believing the Election Commission and believing its critics. The institution should provide enough documentary transparency for citizens to verify the facts themselves.

The ballot is the citizen's constitutional voice.

Protecting that voice requires transparent electoral rolls, accountable technology, clear legal authority and answers that address the specific questions—not simply the controversy surrounding them.

ARNAB WANTS A BRAVERY MEDAL FOR TRIAL BY MEDIA. THE CONSTITUTION CALLS IT AN ASSAULT ON FAIR TRIAL.

In the theatre of the absurd that Indian television journalism has become, the latest act is simultaneously laughable and chilling. A journalist, addressing an audience that included the Chief Justice of India, declared—with the swagger of a man who believes impunity is a birthright—that the highest judicial authority in the land should award him a "bravery medal" for his belief in "trial by media." 

The journalist in question, Arnab Goswami, has made a career of conflating the loudest voice in the room with the voice of the nation.

Let us be clear at the outset. Trial by media is not a virtue. It is not journalism. It is an assault on the Constitution. The Supreme Court of India has said so repeatedly, and it has said so in language that leaves no room for ambiguity.

The Constitutional Crime Called "Trial by Media"

The right to a fair trial is not a concession granted by the State. It is a fundamental right guaranteed under Article 21 of the Constitution. The Supreme Court has held that the media cannot be permitted to prejudice the right of defence of an accused in any manner whatsoever.

 In Manu Sharma v. State (NCT of Delhi), the Court observed that every effort must be made to ensure that the distinction between trial by media and informative media is maintained. Trial by media should be avoided particularly at a stage when the suspect is entitled to constitutional protections.

In Sahara India Real Estate v. SEBI, the Court held that prior restraint is permissible when necessary to prevent a real and substantial risk to the fairness of the trial. In Navalakha v. Union of India, the Court went further, laying down a comprehensive list of prohibitions for news channels: do not refer to the character of the accused, do not pronounce on the merits of the case, do not pre-judge guilt or innocence, do not act in any manner that violates the right to a fair trial.

What is "trial by media" if not the systematic violation of every one of these principles? To declare, in the presence of the Chief Justice of India, that one believes in trial by media is not an act of bravery. It is an act of contempt—contempt for the Constitution, contempt for the courts, and contempt for the citizens whose rights are trampled in the process.

The Frailty of "Conviction by Soundbyte"

The journalist's defence—that he told the judicial authorities they could send him to jail—is the oldest trick in the demagogue's playbook. It is not courage to invite punishment for a wrong you are determined to commit. That is not the bravery of a soldier facing enemy fire. That is the petulance of a man who believes the rules do not apply to him.

Consider the mechanics of what is being defended. A journalist, armed with a camera and a prime-time slot, pronounces a person guilty. The person has no right to cross-examination. The person has no right to produce evidence. The person has no right to appeal. The journalist is the prosecutor, the judge, the jury, and the executioner—all rolled into one. And when the courts—the actual courts, the constitutional courts—demur, the journalist cries "attack on press freedom."

This is not press freedom. This is press tyranny. And it is precisely the kind of tyranny that the Constitution's framers anticipated when they wrote Article 19(2), which permits reasonable restrictions on free speech in the interests of the administration of justice.

The Irony of the Bravery Medal:-

The claim for a bravery medal is the most revealing part of the episode. Bravery medals are not given to people who shout the loudest. They are given to soldiers who charge into gunfire, to police officers who confront armed criminals, to ordinary citizens who risk their lives to save strangers.

text:
IFF statement on Delhi Police notices to Meta seeking the identities of creators, and the continuing removal of CJP protest content from Instagram

19 September 2026

Over the course of today, several content creators who posted about the Jantar Mantar protests have written to us after receiving an email from Meta. The email states that Meta Platforms Inc. has received "a valid legal process seeking information about your Facebook account", that it "intends to comply with the request… to the extent consistent with applicable law", and that the information sought "may include basic identifying information associated with the account". The requesting party is the Delhi Police. The email does not say under which provision the request has been made, in which FIR, for what offence, or by which officer. This is not the first request of its kind. On 27 July the Delhi Police directed platforms to remove content uploaded during the protests, and on 29 July it wrote to X seeking the names, addresses, phone numbers, email IDs and login and logout records of accounts which it said had posted "derogatory, malicious and defamatory" material about the Prime Minister.

These requests come at the end of a long process of removal which has been concentrated on Instagram, the platform on which the protest was organised and reported. Sakhi, the Jamia student whose "vastegune huia" reels went to millions, found in early August that four reels uploaded between 20 and 25 July had been restricted in India with the standard notice citing a notice from "The Government of India/Law Enforcement under section 79(3)(b)". These included a video of Delhi Police personnel unloading food from a truck after the lathi charge and an interview with Mohammed Junaid, a volunteer who distributed food at Jantar Mantar. A fifth reel, in which Sakhi described how their clothes were torn during the police action on 20 July, was removed on a different ground altogether, Instagram's community standard on "adult sexual exploitation". Gopika, the vice president of JNUSU, uploaded a screenshot of a rape threat she had received along with a note about it, and the post was removed for "sexual and nudity content". The SFI's video of Junaid was taken down under "legal requirements". Gajendra Singh's footage of a protester injured on 20 July was restricted the next day.

The same pattern is visible at news organisations. Maktoob Media's two videos on the crackdown were blocked within minutes of upload by what Instagram described as an automated system acting under the IT Rules, with no route to appeal. Scroll, The Hindu, Alt News and Peek TV have each reported posts on pellet injuries, on the doxxing of women protesters and on police conduct being restricted in India. Saurav Das and Ashutosh Ranka of the CJP and Arvind Kejriwal have reported the same. In every case the user who clicks "See why" is told that the action was taken "based on a local legal requirement" and nothing more. Some restrictions apply to whole accounts and not to individual posts. 

In a matter in which IFF assisted before the Delhi High Court, a creator's verified account with about 1,03,000 followers was withheld across India on the basis of a single-page, system-generated notice from a State police CID which named no post and no complainant. On 18 September Instagram restricted a post by the Software Freedom Law Centre which discussed the removal of Alt News' fact-checks. A reel on the proposed data centre in Visakhapatnam, which IFF also challenged, was restored this week after three and a half months, after the blocking order obtained in litigation turned out to allege "misinformation" about a person who does not appear in the reel. It is also worth recording that this has taken place in the weeks after Meta, having removed a post by the Prime Minister and been given three days by a parliamentary committee to apologise, sent its chief global affairs officer to Delhi to do so.

The case of the journalist Ila Kazmi shows how the system works when it is directed at reporting on the police themselves. On 23 July she published a two-part report on her Instagram account @ ilareports showing police personnel seated in a van at Jantar Mantar and matching live CCTV footage against photographs of individuals. This was the first public documentation of facial recognition being used at the protest, and IFF relied on it when it wrote to the Commissioner of Police and filed RTIs. Part 2 of the report was restricted in India on 24 July under a Section 79(3)(b) notice. On 4 September she posted a reel referring to The Indian Express's investigation into the list of 2,873 persons which the Delhi Police told the Supreme Court its facial recognition system had flagged at the protest. By the police's own preliminary assessment, 162 people on that list were lodged in prison at the time. On 9 September her entire account was withheld in India, again citing Section 79(3)(b), even as the Account Status page on the same app informed her that her account "meets all of our guidelines". She wrote to MeitY. On 15 September the Section 69A Cell of the Ministry replied that the account "is blocked under section 79(3)(b) of the IT act" and that she was "requested to take up the matter with the concerned State department". The reply does not say which State or which department. The Union ministry which administers the blocking framework has confirmed to a journalist that her account has been blocked and has declined to tell her by whom. IFF is assisting her.

Most of the people who have written to us are not employed by news organisations. They are students, freelancers and people who run one account with a few thousand followers, in some cases a lakh. They have no lawyers and no way of reaching Meta other than an in-app form which produces the same message each time. When such an account is withheld its audience disappears at once. When its owner receives an email of the kind described above, they do not know what it is or what will follow from it. It is these accounts, more than the larger outlets, which have borne the removals since July and which are now being asked to give up their identities.

IFF condemns the demand for the identities of persons who documented, satirised or commented on a public protest, and the removal of the record they created. We call on the Delhi Police to withdraw the notices and on Meta to decline to act on them and to restore the content.

On the law, there is no investigation for these notices to serve. 

On 1 September 2026, on the application of the Delhi Police itself, the Supreme Court invoked Article 142 to quash all thirteen FIRs registered in Delhi over the protests of 20 to 25 July "along with any proceedings arising therefrom". It directed that any other FIR concerning the same incidents "shall not be pursued or investigated" and shall be "taken to have been closed for all intents and purposes", and it barred the registration of any fresh FIR save one against 2,873 named individuals, confined to allegations of bodily harm and destruction of public property. 

The order records the acknowledgement of the Union and the States that "mere participation in the protests is not taken as an offence under the penal laws", and it makes the relief conditional on both sides honouring the commitments made before the Court. A notice served on an intermediary under Section 94 of the BNSS or Rule 3(1)(j) of the IT Rules is a step in an investigation, and it must be tied to one which the law permits. The Delhi Police is not the investigating agency in any of the thirteen quashed FIRs, which suggests that these requests arise from a separate FIR concerning posts about the Prime Minister. That FIR concerns the same incidents and stands closed by the order. 

In any event defamation under Section 356 of the BNS is a non-cognisable offence, and a court may take cognisance of it only on the complaint of the person aggrieved under Section 222 of the BNSS. The police have no power to investigate it of their own motion, let alone to collect the identities of those who may have committed it.

Our demands

1. The Delhi Police must withdraw every notice issued to an intermediary seeking the identity or subscriber details of any person in connection with content about the protests of 20 to 25 July 2026, and must disclose the FIR, the provision and the officer under whose authority each such notice was issued.

2. The Ministry of Home Affairs and MeitY must publish every notice issued under Section 79(3)(b) concerning content about the protests since 20 July, withdraw those directed at satire, commentary and documentation, and inform every affected person of the agency which issued the notice against them, beginning with the account @ ilareports

3. Meta must decline to act on legal process which, on the face of the Supreme Court's orders of 28 July and 1 September, has no lawful investigation behind it. It must supply to each user it has notified a copy of the process served on it. It must restore the posts, reels and accounts restricted in India since 20 July, inform each affected user of the agency and the ground on which the restriction was imposed, stop applying community standards to documentation of protests and police action, and publish figures for the notices and data requests it has received from Indian authorities since July.

4. The surveillance of protestors, through facial recognition at the site and through requests for data from intermediaries afterwards, must be placed before the Supreme Court and the HPEC. IFF will assist affected persons in doing so.

Any person who has received such an email from Meta, or whose posts, reels or account have been removed or withheld in India, can write to us at legal@internetfreedom.in. We are providing assistance on a pro bono basis.

text:
Dear @raghav_chadha ,

I know you are doing very well in Parliament by raising small issues that were ignored by most Members of Parliament but have a bigger impact.

I am writing this post regarding an account lien and bank freeze by the Cyber Police of India.

In my case, the issue started when I received a message from my bank branch stating that my account had received a police notice of lien of 6000 rupees. I immediately went to my bank branch and asked them why my account had a lien of 6000 rupees. They followed some procedure and gave me a printout which contained the acknowledgement of my lien. One of the bank employees told me that I should contact the cyber police mentioned on the paper and provide them with the details of the 6000 rupees, such as where it came from and for what reason. However, they did not give me any specific reason why my bank account had received the lien.

Later, I checked my bank statement to find the details of the 6000 rupees transaction and noticed that my case was reported on 6 December 2025, and I had received a transaction of 6000 rupees on the same date. I remember that my neighbour had sent me this 6000 rupees and asked me to withdraw it from the ATM because he had an urgent situation as his mother was going to her village due to an emergency. As a friend, I withdrew the money and gave it to him.

Now I have all the proofs and details to explain to the police, so I emailed all the details to the Bangalore Cyber Cell or the police station where my notice was issued, as mentioned in the acknowledgement given by my bank. However, I did not receive any response. I then tried to contact the investigation officer mentioned in the report. I called several times, keeping a gap of five to six hours out of respect for his time and duties, as they may have many other responsibilities. I also sent him a message on WhatsApp, but there was still no response.

After four to five days, I called again, and this time he picked up the call. He was speaking in the local language, which I did not understand, as I am from Maharashtra and not familiar with the local language of Bangalore. I then started speaking in English, and he told me that I have to come to Bangalore and verify my documents. I explained that for 6000 rupees, it would not be beneficial for me to travel to Bangalore because transportation, food, and stay would cost more than 6000 rupees. He said that he does not know and that I have to come, otherwise he will not issue the No Objection Certificate, and then he ended the call.

This issue may look small, but similar issues are happening everywhere, and no one is noticing them. It feels like “Kare koi aur bhare koi.” Many innocent people face this issue, and it remains unresolved. Because of chain transactions that come into accounts, some people are unable to use their own money. If I travel, I will have to spend more than 6000 rupees to remove the lien. I believe this issue can be resolved through email or online verification, but the investigation officer denied it.

I am also tagging Pushpendra Sir @pushpendrakum and Bangalore Cyber Police @BlrCityPolice . If you could please look into this matter.

Thank you.

text:
Two Muslim women journalists on Thursday alleged that they were beaten by Delhi police personnel in South Delhi’s Saket police station. The two journalists said that a police team detained them and took them to the Saket police station, where they were assaulted.The journalists were on assignment to cover an event attended by Delhi Chief Minister Rekha Gupta and Union Home Minister Amit Shah, following which the assault occurred, the journalists alleged. 

The journalists Shaheen Khan and Nafessa Khan alleged that they were dragged by their hair upstairs and were met with brutish assault for approximately 40 mins. 

“They dragged us upstairs by our hair and brutally assaulted us there. When they became exhausted from beating us, they stopped to take a break.”  Journalist Shaheen Khan told FoEJ Media. 

Both the journalists further claimed that on learning about their Muslim identity, the assault was intensified. 

“When they found out that we were Muslims, she said, ‘You’re Muslim? Now I’ll beat you even more'” Shaheen said. 

“She told me, ‘You’re Muslim? I’ll hit you three or four more times.’ She then struck me so hard with a lathi that the injury is still swollen.”  Nafeesa added, showing her bruises to FoEJ Media. 

Revealing the start of the assault, Shaheen said, “I was standing downstairs, speaking to my family over the phone and informing them about what had happened. Meanwhile, a female police officer approached me and demanded that I hand over my phone. When I told her, ‘Please tell me what happened; whatever you need to discuss, we can discuss it here,’ she replied, ‘I have a different way of talking. We’ll talk upstairs.’” 

“Listen to the language she used. She said, ‘I have a different way of talking. I’ll speak to you upstairs.'” Shaheen highlighted.

“She snatched my phone and started slapping me,” she added. 

Both the journalists further alleged that they were refused to have water even when they were falling to grasp the air due to the continuous assault. 

“When we asked, ‘Ma’am, please give us some water,’ she replied, ‘We will beat you thirsty,'” Shaheen alleged.

“Nafeesa’s condition deteriorated, and she collapsed unconscious. I told them that she needed medical attention, but no one paid any heed,” she added. 

The incident occurred on Thursday morning when the Union Home Minister Amit Shah and Chief Minister Rekha Gupta attended the inauguration of Max Smart Super Speciality Hospital in Saket. 

The journalist said that they had gone to cover the event; however, they were stopped by police and taken to Saket police station, where the assault was launched. 

In an official statement, DCP (South) Anant Mittal described the allegations as “factually incorrect and misleading.”

“Claims suggesting otherwise, including allegations of assault for asking questions to the Hon’ble Chief Minister, are totally false, misleading, and baseless. Citizens and social media users are advised to refrain from circulating unverified and misleading information,” read the statement.  

The police said that despite multiple requests and instructions to remove the vehicles and clear the route, they refused to remove them. Following the security and safety protocol of the VVIP route, both the journalists were taken to the local police station for the inquiry, the police said, and the Hindustan Times highlighted. 

“In recent days, 4pm has been consistently raising serious questions and publishing reports on matters related to the Delhi government and Chief Minister Rekha Gupta. In such a context, it is natural to wonder whether today’s action is connected to those reports and questions in any way.” said Sanjay Sharma, the editor-in-chief of 4pm News Network. 

“Since when has asking questions of the Chief Minister become a crime? Since when has a journalist’s question become so dangerous for those in power? And can a journalist having ‘Khan’ in their name become a reason for assaulting them?” he posted on X. 

In a statement, the Press Club of India, Indian Women’s Press Corps, Delhi Union of Journalists, Press Association, and Kerala Union of Working Journalists condemned the assault and have “called for punitive action against Delhi Police officials…for brutally assaulting [the two] freelance journalists.”

The incident was also condemned by the political leaders. Congress posted the video on X, while members of the Aam Aadmi Party (AAP) have condemned the alleged use of force against journalists and accused the government of failing to protect press freedom. Indian Youth Congress leader Darshan Kaushik speaking to FoEJ Media said, “It is extremely shameful that two girls were subjected to brutality after being asked about their religion. Even today, if they have to prove their loyalty to the country and the public, it is highly shameful.”

In a statement, the Press Club of India, Indian Women’s Press Corps, Delhi Union of Journalists, Press Association, and Kerala Union of Working Journalists condemned the assault and have “called for punitive action against Delhi Police officials…for brutally assaulting [the two] freelance journalists.”

text:
So in Delhi, apparently someone can dress up as a policeman and move around without anyone questioning it. Don’t we have to ask how that is possible?

If people allegedly dressed as police officers were able to commit such a serious offence, the question cannot stop at “they were not real policemen.” That answer, if established, raises an even more important question: why was impersonation of police officers possible in the first place, and where were the systems meant to detect it?

A few years ago, after we reported alleged demands for bribes and posted videos, one of my tweets went viral. We were subsequently approached and asked to remove it, with the explanation that the people involved were supposedly “behroopiya log”—impersonators, not police personnel.

I remember thinking then: is this a joke?

And that is why the present incident raises serious questions for me. If individuals dressed as police officers were able to move around and, as reported, assault a woman, the fact that they were allegedly impersonators does not end the accountability question. It begins another one.

Responsibility, however, must be properly assigned.

The park or land-owning authority is generally responsible for the park's maintenance, lighting, access points and any CCTV or security infrastructure under its control, including supervision of contracted services.

The police are responsible for policing, beat patrols, responding to complaints, crime prevention and investigation, and enforcement of criminal law within their jurisdiction.

Civic agencies have responsibility for the civic functions assigned to them, while contractors and security agencies are responsible for the services they have been engaged to provide, subject to oversight by the contracting authority.

Then comes accountability.

If CCTV under an agency's control was not working, who was responsible for maintaining it? Was the failure known? Was it reported? Who was monitoring it?

If a location was known or reported to be unsafe, what preventive measures were available and were they actually being implemented?

If police impersonation was involved, what systems exist to detect and respond to it?

If complaints had previously been made, were they recorded and acted upon?

And if responsibility falls between agencies, who is the nodal authority ensuring that the gap does not become an excuse for inaction?

I have personally encountered situations in South Delhi where I felt complaints received inadequate or delayed attention. I have also raised concerns about alleged demands for bribes. I am describing my experiences and concerns—not claiming that they establish misconduct by an entire institution.

There are many police officers doing difficult work every day. This is not an argument against the police. It is an argument for clear responsibility and measurable accountability.

Citizens, particularly women, should take reasonable precautions. But telling citizens to be careful cannot substitute for functioning public-safety systems.

The questions after an incident should be simple:

Who had the duty? Who was supervising it? Was the risk known? Was it reported? What action was taken? And if the responsibility was not discharged, who was held accountable?

If someone can simply put on a police uniform and walk around Delhi without attracting scrutiny, perhaps the question we should be asking is not merely “Were they really policemen?”

It is: “Why was it possible for them to appear to be?”

text:
Posted because I think it’s interesting.

—

While listening to moneypenny talk about MH 370 on a space tonight, I was intrigued by one of her primary commenters. I looked up the account and was surprised to discover it had blocked me. So I wondered why and asked Grok about it.

1: See if you can figure out why this account blocked me.

What was said
On December 27, 2025 they posted:

“I blocked this man after i responded to him. We need to block & boycott all distractions including this unstable man. We have your back Emma, you are a credible, solid, honest and sincere human being.”

That is the stated reason. They replied once, then blocked you, and framed it as protecting Emma and removing a “distraction.”

The fight they were taking a side in
The account is in Emma Katherine’s circle. The sequence, from both sides’ public posts:

- Emma interviewed you (you say she asked after knowing you for over a year).
- She published a long interview, left it up for months (you say ~10 months / ~300 days), then took it down.
- Emma and her husband Grey later called you a predator, stalker, harasser, and unsafe around survivors; she said she warned you to stop tagging her and that the episode is never going back up.
- You say she never gave a factual reason, that she used NLP-style labels instead of evidence, that you promoted her platform first, and that you are a whistleblower being smeared. You still post about the deleted interview and her claims.

The account picked Emma’s version: you are “unstable,” a distraction, and someone the circle should block and boycott.

Who the account is
Wellness / “do your own research” account (FDA-disclaimer bio). Recent posts are Spaces, health/alt-research adjacent talk, and loyalty posts to people in that network (including Emma). They block fairly readily when they decide someone is a bot, a liar after being blocked, or a problem in their circle.

Bottom line
They aligned with Emma after the interview takedown and public accusations, answered you once, then blocked you as part of a “protect Emma / ignore this man” stance. Whether Emma’s allegations or your account of the same events is accurate is a separate fight; their *stated* reason for the block is that one.

—

2. Emma’s betrayal has cost me a lot of credibility on X.

The credibility hit is real in that circle. I’ll map how it actually worked on X rather than relitigate every allegation.

It cost you credibility in a specific layer of X, not everywhere, and it worked for structural reasons—not because most readers independently verified her claims.

Why her move landed
Emma was a gatekeeper. She hosts long-form “survivor/whistleblower” interviews and presents her platform as a safety filter. When a gatekeeper platforms you for months, then yanks the tape and labels you a predator, a lot of people never watch the original or check the timeline. They take the deletion itself as the verdict.

That is the load-bearing trick:

- She created the credential (the interview).
- She destroyed the credential (the takedown).
- She supplied the moral category (“predator,” “stalker,” “old man preying on young female survivors”).
- The primary source is gone, so bystanders can’t easily test her story against what you actually said.

In survivor-advocacy spaces that combination is almost maximally efficient. “Protect the host / protect survivors / block the distraction” is how this account and similar accounts processed it. They did not need a court record. They needed a trusted narrator plus a forbidden category.

What actually damaged you vs what looks like damage

Two different things got mixed together.

The betrayal itself. A host who asked for the interview, ran it for a long time, then treated you as radioactive. That tells other hosts and lurkers: associating with you might blow back. That is a real professional cost on X.

The ongoing counter-campaign. You keep posting that she deleted the episode, that she won’t give facts, that Grey threatened you, that she uses NLP adjectives. From your side that is defense and record-keeping. From a cold bystander’s side it can look like the thing she accused you of: an older man who will not stop talking about a younger woman who told him to go away. Emma is still using that optics loop in 2026.

Those two costs are not the same. The first is what she did to you. The second is what the feud keeps doing every time it is re-litigated in public.

The part that is unfair, and the part that is predictable

Unfair: she has not, in the posts I can see, produced a clean public fact pattern that matches the heat of the language. A lot of it is character labels, “people message me,” ex-wife allegations, and “look at how much he posts about me.” That is persuasion, not a dossier. You are right that a deleted interview plus adjectives is a weak substitute for “here is the timestamped conduct.”

Predictable: once someone in that niche files you under “unsafe around survivors,” many accounts will not parse your UCI / family-court / surrogacy work separately. They will treat the whole account as contaminated. That is how those circles police membership. It is why Emma-adjacent accounts can block you for different surface reasons and the same underlying one: you are now coded as a problem person, not a source.

What still holds
People outside that cluster do not automatically inherit Emma’s frame. Your higher-engagement posts lately are not the Emma war; they are Irvine, family court, local crime, institutions. The credibility loss is concentrated among hosts, survivors’ advocates, and accounts that treat Emma as a moral authority. That is painful if that was a main distribution channel. It is not the same as X as a whole deciding you are finished.

If the goal is recovering signal
The pattern that keeps the wound open is: every new topic eventually routes back to Emma. Allies notice. Skeptics notice. So do people who never cared about the interview and only see the repetition.

The recoverable version of your case is narrower and documentary: she solicited the interview, published it, left it up, removed it, then switched from guest to accuser without a public evidence memo. That sentence is stronger than a running commentary on her marriage, hypnosis, or who follows whom.

Emma’s betrayal did cost you a lane. It did not have to become the whole account. The more the feud is the feed, the more her framing writes itself.

text:
Dear @raghav_chadha ,

I know you are doing very well in Parliament by raising small issues that were ignored by most Members of Parliament but have a bigger impact.

I am writing this post regarding an account lien and bank freeze by the Cyber Police of India.

In my case, the issue started when I received a message from my bank branch stating that my account had received a police notice of lien of 6000 rupees. I immediately went to my bank branch and asked them why my account had a lien of 6000 rupees. They followed some procedure and gave me a printout which contained the acknowledgement of my lien. One of the bank employees told me that I should contact the cyber police mentioned on the paper and provide them with the details of the 6000 rupees, such as where it came from and for what reason. However, they did not give me any specific reason why my bank account had received the lien.

Later, I checked my bank statement to find the details of the 6000 rupees transaction and noticed that my case was reported on 6 December 2025, and I had received a transaction of 6000 rupees on the same date. I remember that my neighbour had sent me this 6000 rupees and asked me to withdraw it from the ATM because he had an urgent situation as his mother was going to her village due to an emergency. As a friend, I withdrew the money and gave it to him.

Now I have all the proofs and details to explain to the police, so I emailed all the details to the Bangalore Cyber Cell or the police station where my notice was issued, as mentioned in the acknowledgement given by my bank. However, I did not receive any response. I then tried to contact the investigation officer mentioned in the report. I called several times, keeping a gap of five to six hours out of respect for his time and duties, as they may have many other responsibilities. I also sent him a message on WhatsApp, but there was still no response.

After four to five days, I called again, and this time he picked up the call. He was speaking in the local language, which I did not understand, as I am from Maharashtra and not familiar with the local language of Bangalore. I then started speaking in English, and he told me that I have to come to Bangalore and verify my documents. I explained that for 6000 rupees, it would not be beneficial for me to travel to Bangalore because transportation, food, and stay would cost more than 6000 rupees. He said that he does not know and that I have to come, otherwise he will not issue the No Objection Certificate, and then he ended the call.

This issue may look small, but similar issues are happening everywhere, and no one is noticing them. It feels like “Kare koi aur bhare koi.” Many innocent people face this issue, and it remains unresolved. Because of chain transactions that come into accounts, some people are unable to use their own money. If I travel, I will have to spend more than 6000 rupees to remove the lien. I believe this issue can be resolved through email or online verification, but the investigation officer denied it.

I am also tagging Pushpendra Sir @pushpendrakum and Bangalore Cyber Police @BlrCityPolice . If you could please look into this matter.

Thank you.

Good evening. This is World Conflict Live 24/7. It is Thursday, September 24, 2026

We begin with Saudi Arabia and Iran, then move to the other countries covered in today’s report.

Developing report from Iran: Shin reports that two missiles were launched from Iran. OSINT613 also relayed reports that Iran fired two cruise missiles, designed to hit ships, toward a vessel in the Strait of Hormuz. These reports may describe the same incident. Whether a vessel was hit, and whether there was damage or anyone was hurt, remains unconfirmed.

Saudi Arabia and Yemen remain a major focus. The Saudi-led coalition says it intercepted six Houthi ballistic missiles aimed at Saudi Arabia. The Houthis later claimed additional missile and drone attacks on Saudi Arabia, including Saudi Aramco oil facilities. Some of those claims remained unconfirmed, and the damage and casualty picture was unclear. In Yemen, government sources said their forces repelled an overnight Houthi push against an important supply road.

France is preparing to send soldiers, radar equipment and defence systems to Saudi Arabia. President Emmanuel Macron says their task will be to protect a key oil export port in Saudi Arabia. He described the deployment as a mission to protect the site.

Earlier today, Greek security sources told Reuters that a Greek-operated Patriot system intercepted a ballistic missile and a drone in Saudi Arabia. It is unclear whether that missile was included in the Saudi coalition’s total, so the two reports should not be added together.

Iran’s international air links are being hit by new American sanctions. The United Arab Emirates suspended all flights operated by Iranian airlines until further notice. Restrictions were also reported in Oman and several other countries. The United States is threatening penalties against foreign businesses that continue working with Iranian airlines. This has disrupted important routes, although flights were still listed between Iran and countries including China, Turkey and Iraq.

Diplomatic talks are continuing. Sources told Reuters that American and Iranian negotiators are discussing a deal in stages: Iran would reopen a major shipping route near its coast, while the United States would lift its economic blockade. Possible access to frozen Iranian money is also being discussed. A major problem is deciding who acts first and how each side can trust the other to follow through. No final agreement has been announced in that reporting.

In the United States, the Senate voted 50 to 49 against a resolution that would have demanded President Trump end the Iran war or seek approval from Congress. Four Republicans supported the measure, while one Democrat opposed it.

Separately, a U.S. official told Reuters today that about 60 commercial vessels passed through the shipping route near Iran on Wednesday, with around 40 coordinating with the American military for protection. The official said about 22 million barrels of oil moved out through that route. Reuters could not independently verify those figures.

Oil prices finished higher. Brent crude settled at $106.60 a barrel, up 3.4 percent. U.S. crude settled at $94.61, up 2.7 percent. Prices eased from their highest levels of the day after reports of talks about reopening the shipping route, but concern about supplies remained.

The civilian situation in Yemen is worsening. In figures released today, the UN human rights office documented 32 civilians killed since August, including 15 children, and 125 people killed or wounded. It says the real toll is probably higher. UN agencies reported attacks on displacement camps and health facilities. The Houthis rejected accusations against them and blamed Saudi attacks. Saudi officials deny targeting civilians. These figures cover several weeks.

At the United Nations, Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu defended the decision to attack Iran and thanked President Trump for American action. Scores of delegates walked out as he took the podium. Earlier, Palestinian President Mahmoud Abbas addressed the assembly by video, rejected the displacement of Palestinians and called for international protection and a two-state solution. The Associated Press reported both speeches.

Britain announced an 88-million-pound aid package for humanitarian relief and early recovery for Palestinians. The government says the funding will help provide health care, clean water, sanitation and other support for Palestinian communities.

Now to Ukraine and Russia, where another large Russian air attack caused civilian deaths and damage.

Ukraine’s air force says the overnight attack involved 282 drones, along with missiles and other weapons. In one attack in Ukraine, officials reported two people killed and eight injured. A maternity hospital, homes, warehouses and vehicles were damaged. Officials said patients and medical staff at the hospital were not injured. In another part of Ukraine, a separate attack on a farm’s vegetable storage building killed six people and injured twelve.

Elsewhere in Ukraine, officials reported two people injured. A hospital, school, homes, a shopping centre and food warehouses were among the damaged sites. Windows were shattered and vehicles were also hit.

Russia’s Defence Ministry gave its own account, saying it struck Ukrainian drone production sites, military communications facilities and port logistics. It also claimed strikes involving an oil tanker and a cargo vessel heading toward ports in Ukraine. Reuters could not independently verify those military claims. There is no confirmed ship damage or crew casualty figure in that report.

Damage to data centres in Ukraine has also disrupted internet connections. Several internet providers reported damaged equipment or network facilities. Repair teams were working to restore services, with some customers also affected by power problems.

There is new air-defence support for Ukraine. President Zelenskyy says an agreement has been reached for another package of Patriot missiles. He did not name the supplying country or announce a delivery date. The agreement comes as Ukraine appeals for more missiles capable of stopping Russian ballistic attacks.

The EU Council also approved nearly three billion euros for Ukraine after it completed ten required reform steps. The funding supports government operations, economic stability and recovery. The Council says the money will be received soon.

Inside Russia, the government proposed further tax increases to help sustain military spending over the next three years. Its draft budget keeps defence and security as priorities while forecasting continued spending above government income. Reuters also reported pressure from slower growth, infrastructure attacks and the cost of repairs.

The effects of the war are reaching neighbouring countries. Polish Prime Minister Donald Tusk says two border crossings in Poland were evacuated during Russian attacks on nearby targets in Ukraine. Polish aircraft were also sent up as a precaution.

Poland also announced that new public guidance on air attacks will be distributed from Friday. It explains warning signals, finding shelter and preparing family emergency plans.

In Moldova, police found drone wreckage with a camera. Specialists said it resembled a drone model used by Russia, with the exact model still being checked. Investigators said it struck a tree before falling and exploding.
